title: Pinwheel Power: Catch the Wind
description: Paper, a pin and a pencil become a spinning wind wheel. Build a pinwheel, label its parts, and learn how moving air becomes turning power — the wind turbine's baby cousin.

body.heading: A wheel that eats wind
paragraphs: Wind is invisible, but a pinwheel makes it visible — every gust shows up as a spin. Your pinwheel is a tiny wind turbine: the same machine that, grown to the size of a building, lights up whole towns. Build one and hold the wind in your hand.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The blades — four folded paper triangles that catch the wind; each one is angled like a tiny sail. The hub — the centre where the blades meet and the pin passes through. The axle — the pin itself, the rod the wheel turns on. The mast — the pencil or stick you hold, which must stay still while the wheel spins free.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: A square of stiff paper or thin card, safety scissors, a ruler and pencil for marking, a dressmaker's pin with a bead head (a grown-up keeps charge of it), a small bead, and a pencil with an eraser end or a wooden stick for the mast.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Mark the square. A grown-up draws two diagonal lines corner to corner. Cut along each line from the corner toward the centre — stopping a thumb's width from the middle. The centre must stay whole.

Step 2 — Fold the blades. Bend every OTHER corner into the centre, so four points meet in the middle. The folds make the angled blades — flat paper would just flap, but angled blades catch the wind and turn it into spin.

Step 3 — Pin the hub. A grown-up pushes the pin through all four folded points and the centre, then through a small bead, then into the pencil's eraser. The bead is a spacer — it holds the wheel away from the mast so it can spin without rubbing.

Step 4 — Catch the wind. Hold the mast still, face the wheel into the breeze (or walk slowly forward), and watch it spin. Turn sideways to the wind: the spin dies. A pinwheel only eats wind that hits its blades face-on.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: Wind is moving air, and moving air pushes. The blades are angled, so the push lands unevenly — stronger on one side of each blade — and that uneven push is what twists the wheel around. Bigger gusts push harder and spin it faster; the spinning speed is a wind-speed meter you can see. Wind turbines work identically: angled blades, a hub, and wind doing the pushing — only their spin turns a generator to make electricity instead of just looking cheerful.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why do the blades have to be ANGLED? What would happen if they were folded perfectly flat?
2. Your pinwheel spins faster and slower as you watch. What is it telling you about the wind?

takeaway: A pinwheel's angled blades catch the wind's push unevenly, turning moving air into spin — the same idea that powers giant wind turbines.
materials: Square of stiff paper or thin card
Dressmaker's pin with a bead head (grown-up keeps it)
Pencil with eraser end or a stick (mast)
supervision: A grown-up handles the pin at every step and supervises the build and the wind testing.
safetyNotes: PINS ARE SHARP: the pin belongs to the grown-up — they do all pinning, carry it point-down, and park it in a pincushion or eraser the moment it is not being used. Never leave a pin in a finished pinwheel unattended where small hands can pull it out.
This build is not for children under 3 (pin and bead are small, sharp hazards); younger siblings watch the spinning from a grown-up's arms.
Outdoor testing: hold the mast, never run with the pinwheel — a fall onto a pin is exactly what the rules are for.
screenFreeExtension: Wind hunt: carry your pinwheel around your garden or street with a grown-up and find the windiest spot — spinning speed is your meter. Mark the champion spot with a ribbon.
